GitLab is the intelligent orchestration platform for DevSecOps. GitLab enables organizations to increase developer productivity, improve operational efficiency, reduce security and compliance risk, and accelerate digital transformation. More than 50 million registered owners and more than 50% of the Fortune 100* trust GitLab to ship better, more secure software faster.

In a recent development, the same principles built into our products are reflected in how our team works: we embrace AI as a core productivity multiplier, with all team members expected to incorporate AI into their daily workflows to drive efficiency, innovation, and impact. GitLab is where careers accelerate, innovation flourishes, and every voice is valued. Our high-performance culture is driven by our values and continuous knowledge exchange, enabling our team members to reach their full potential while collaborating with industry leaders to solve complex problems. Co-create the future with us as we build technology that transforms how the world develops software.

Fortune 100 refers to the top 20% ranked companies in the 2025 Fortune 500 list, published in June 2025. Fortune and Fortune Media IP Limited are not affiliated with, and do not endorse products or services of GitLab.

Recent findings suggest that as a Candidate Experience Specialist, you'll shape how candidates experience GitLab from first touch through offer and handoff to our People Operations team. You'll be a key partner to Recruiters, hiring managers, and recruiting leadership, helping them execute hiring plans, coordinate interviews, and maintain accurate, transparent processes in our applicant tracking system and GitLab repositories. You'll act as a brand ambassador who embodies our values in every interaction, ensuring candidates receive timely, thoughtful communication and a consistent, high quality experience across a high volume of roles. You’ll focus on building strong relationships with hiring teams, improving and standardizing coordination workflows, and supporting GitLab's goal of hiring a qualified, diverse, and motivated team in our all-remote, global environment.

According to recent reports, the Candidate Experience team partners with Recruiters, hiring managers, and People Operations to run a smooth, consistent, and inclusive hiring process across GitLab's all-remote, global organization. You'll join a collaborative group that coordinates interview logistics, manages candidate flow in our applicant tracking system, and supports offer and onboarding handoffs so candidates and hiring teams have a clear, organized experience at every stage. The team works asynchronously across time zones, using GitLab and shared documentation to stay aligned while handling high-volume hiring. Our focus is on refining processes, maintaining accurate data, and acting as brand ambassadors for GitLab's values in every candidate interaction.

Please note that we welcome interest from candidates with varying levels of experience; many successful candidates do not meet every single requirement. Additionally, studies have shown that people from underrepresented groups are less likely to apply to a job unless they meet every single qualification. If you're excited about this role, please apply and allow our recruiters to assess your application.

In a recent development, country Hiring Guidelines: GitLab hires new team members in countries around the world. All of our roles are remote, however some roles may carry specific location-based eligibility requirements. Our Talent Acquisition team can help answer any questions about location after starting the recruiting process.

GitLab is proud to be an equal opportunity workplace and is an affirmative action employer. GitLab’s policies and practices relating to recruitment, employment, career development and advancement, promotion, and retirement are based solely on merit, regardless of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex (including pregnancy, lactation, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression), national origin, age, citizenship, marital status, mental or physical disability, genetic information (including family medical history), discharge status from the military, protected veteran status (which includes disabled veterans, recently separated veterans, active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans, and Armed Forces service medal veterans), or any other basis protected by law. GitLab will not tolerate discrimination or harassment based on any of these characteristics. See also GitLab’s EEO Policy and EEO is the Law. If you have a disability or special need that requires accommodation, please let us know during the recruiting process.

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

From the rollout of newly introduced lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the tech giant. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

Recent findings suggest that dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

Industry observers note that little discussed, however, were the tech giant’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, remarked that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

It has been revealed that “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred said. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

Sources indicate that the meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

It has been revealed that “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter noted. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the manufacturer can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by New Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

In a recent development, many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, remarked earlier this month.

In a recent development, “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant said. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

Sources indicate that trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

“They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” stated the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

It has been revealed that readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

Sources indicate that this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

— James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

In a recent development, given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

In a recent development, “It is vital that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter stated. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a new model to help customers make better decisions.”.

According to recent reports, in recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection tech giant Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building fresh audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

In a recent development, such a reality is already playing out in Washington, remarked Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the tech giant’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

Industry observers note that “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred said. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its newly introduced AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “organization’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

Sources indicate that “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch new brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

The insights into the company’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

“The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred remarked. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

It has been revealed that hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he mentioned, the firm seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

It has been revealed that “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch mentioned during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”.

Building fresh audiences is critical as the tech giant works to claw itself out of debt, said Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

“Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri said. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

Mark Keierleber is an independent investigative journalist who most recently reported on media, bias, and algorithms for Straight Arrow News.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve.
  • You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

In a recent development, kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

According to recent reports, you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

Product, on packaging, launches, and roadmap input.

RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing presently works at Kit.

Sources indicate that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action plan on how we can win these creators.

First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure debuts that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

Pricing and packaging input for a latest tier or add-on (nice to have).

7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

Industry observers note that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

In a recent development, treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

Wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

It has been revealed that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

Sources indicate that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

Recent findings suggest that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

Industry observers note that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

Recent findings suggest that we usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

Hiring manager interview (45 min).

Sources indicate that we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

Recent findings suggest that we value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Graphite flagged 55% of the consumers who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.
  • Among the people it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.
  • Recent findings suggest that the growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Graphite flagged 55% of the consumers who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

Among the people it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

Recent findings suggest that the growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

The agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and says it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

To test the model, the manufacturer manually inspected 43 of the customers it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also says that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

Four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

One account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

Over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from people who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from consumers it flagged as likely promoters.

In a recent development, according to the write-up, consumers frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

In a recent development, the citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by customers. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

The agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also said the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

According to recent reports, graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit consumers weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

It has been revealed that graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the company says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something newly introduced?

These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

Taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely newly introduced kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase.

By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:.

Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape.

It has been revealed that this trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

It has been revealed that and for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous new rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

In a recent development, but the new Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for big dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

Stations in Fresh Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Newly introduced Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

Sources indicate that the bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Upcoming Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, mentioned NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also notable to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story. #192677. Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
📖 Baca

Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature.
  • Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.
  • It has been revealed that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature. The expansion unifies many of Google’s disparate products and services into a single personalized search experience. This upgrade represents a profound change to Google’s Search experience and is likely among the most consequential changes to SEO.

Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.

It has been revealed that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we’re introducing more personally relevant responses, so it’s easier to find just what you need.”.

Industry observers note that some SEOs objected to characterizing Personal Intelligence as something that is about Search, explaining that Personal Intelligence is about Gemini, AI Mode, and AI Overviews. That view can be justified because Google’s announcement is somewhat ambiguous.

Industry observers note that google’s announcement uses the upper-case word Search sixteen times. That seems to be a clear signal that Personal Intelligence affects Search.

“A more tailored Google Search that’s uniquely yours….

…Get more helpful Search responses….

…Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence….

…bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

The following passage seems to unambiguously paint the rollout as affecting Search:.

“Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

Recent findings suggest that the above passage clearly separates AI Mode from Search. Yet, other passages reference AI Mode in Search, introducing a certain amount of ambiguity. An argument can be made that this does not affect Search, but there’s a strong counter-argument there, too.

Google’s announcement ties AI Overviews and AI Mode responses to recent Search contexts, meaning that contextual data from Search can be shared to AIO and AI Mode:.

“You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context.”.

And in another passage Google explains that the contextual data from the Gemini App can be shared with AI Mode in Search:.

“In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.”.

“So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.”.

So it looks like the context data flows from Search to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as from the Gemini App to AI Mode in Search.

The announcement identifies six connected apps:.

But Personal Intelligence is about a whole lot more. It’s about the transformation of disparate services and products into what Google CEO, Sundar Pichai, described in October 2026 as one unified search experience that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

According to recent reports, “I expect our agents to provide that unifying experience across these products. In fact, that agentic layer, rather than try to converge or think about different products and how they come together, I think the agentic layer naturally ends up doing that, right?

Because your agents, they’re running in the cloud, they’re running 24/7, they have your context. And so they can pick up things where you left off.

It has been revealed that so you can start a task in some place. You go to the other place. Your agent has that context for you.

So I think the agentic layer offers us a chance to bring a unified product experience better than ever before.”.

Google’s Personal Intelligence was first announced as a paid Gemini App beta feature in January 2026, which was expanded to AI Mode in search about a week later, initially supporting Gmail and Google Photos as an opt-in Search Labs experiment.

In March it was expanded to free tier owners in the United States and within a few months it was available in 200 countries and 98 languages.

Sources indicate that google declared the expansion of the range of information AI Mode can draw on through Personal Intelligence so that now it includes Google Wallet data, files stored in Google Drive, and Gemini conversations. Google also announced increased personalization of AI Overviews and AI Mode based on recent search activity.

According to recent reports, opt-in connectivity of Google Wallet to AI Mode is beginning to roll out. This is really big and ties into Sundar Pichai’s vision of Search becoming increasingly focused on helping owners accomplish tasks. Google Wallet aggregates data from linked accounts like Gmail and partner apps.

It has been revealed that google Wallet affects travel (like airline tickets), finance, commerce, event tickets, plus sensitive data (in some regions) like drivers license, and health insurance cards. When this feature is enabled, Google Wallet automatically scans incoming emails to import boarding passes, event tickets, loyalty cards, and shipping updates.

Now all of that is connected with Personal Intelligence.

Connectivity to AI Mode is coming in the next few weeks. Google declared that connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence will enable AI Mode to pull information from across stored Google Drive documents, spreadsheets, and PDFs to provide personalized responses and assist users with projects, planning, and decision-making.

“With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation strategy ahead of tax season.”.

Personal Intelligence will be sharing Gemini conversational context between the Gemini app and AI Mode within the next few weeks. Search personalization will come in the form of more personally relevant responses based on recent search activity.

Sources indicate that personalization transparency is coming soon. Owners will be able to see what personal context AI Mode used to generate a response and correct that information.

Transformation Of Google Search Personal Intelligence represents a fundamental change in how Google Search (and/or AI Mode in Search) can respond to consumers, incorporating knowledge about their activities alongside information from the web.

Unification Of Google’s Products And Services Previously disparate Google products and services are now increasingly part of a unified, personalized search experience.

Google’s Agentic Layer The expansion of Personal Intelligence is consistent with Sundar Pichai’s vision of a unified, task-based experience that maintains context across Google’s products.

Sharing Of Contextual Data The sharing of personal and conversational context across Google’s products enables consumers to continue activities without having to start over.

Expansion Beyond Information Discovery The integration of additional data sources enables Google to become increasingly useful for planning, decision-making, and accomplishing tasks.

Increasingly Personalized Search Experiences Search responses are becoming more specific to individual people, a change that SEOs need to really think about and integrate into how what they do fits into this new multi-dimensional level of Search.

How To Opt Out Of Google Personal Intelligence Google is giving owners greater insight into and control over the personal context used to generate AI Mode responses. Users can opt out or in from Personal Intelligence here.

Google Search is increasingly an experience that’s as much about what Google knows about the user and what they want to accomplish as it is about what the user is searching for. This is arguably one of the most consequential moments in SEO that I have experienced in my nearly 30 years of experience in SEO.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence. We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning newly introduced ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

    Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

    We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

    Sources indicate that fingerprint is looking for a Technical Product Manager (P3) to help turn product strategy into clear, well-executed product delivery. This role is ideal for someone who is building strong product management fundamentals, enjoys working closely with engineering and design, and is energized by keeping product work organized, well-documented, and moving toward release.

    It has been revealed that in this role, you will own specific product features or workstreams under the guidance of a Sr Technical Product Manager. You will help translate product intent into clear user stories, jobs-to-be-done, acceptance criteria, release aims, documentation, and operational updates. You will work across Product, Engineering, Design, Product Analytics, Customer Success, Sales, and Product Marketing to ensure product records are accurate, dependencies are visible, stakeholders are informed, and shipped work meets the expected customer and business outcomes.

    This role blends TPM expectations with the Delivery Product Owner operating model: the Sr TPM sets product direction, priorities, success metrics, and major tradeoffs; the TPM helps ensure that direction becomes shippable, well-understood, and well-supported product increments.

    A successful TPM at Fingerprint:.

    At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team. Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

    Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $126k - $170k.

Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote company and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas.     ProPublica notes November has been the busiest month ever for its tips line.

    Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”?

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEProPublica wanted to find more sources in the federal government. So it brought a truck.Neel DhaneshaMarch 31, 2025ProPublica reported on potential aims to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.”.

    But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece:.

    In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Initiative.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

    The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer.

    According to recent reports, sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint.

    Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip.

    According to recent reports, “That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.”.

    We’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting.

    Recent findings suggest that proPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera noted. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line.

    RELATED ARTICLEHow to leak to a journalistLaura Hazard OwenApril 2, 2025“We have to attribute some of this surge to our efforts to get out into the world and show people that we’re listening and that they can trust us with their knowledge — from working with ad companies in Washington, D.C., to get our tips line on bus shelters, to flyering outside of conferences, and events with sources that could help our reporting needs,” she stated.

    Recent findings suggest that during a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by.

    “We’re always looking for ways to reach the people we need to reach, in the places they’re likeliest to be, based on our reporting needs,” Mel Kramer, engagement team product manager, said. “A good tips line is both staffed and comes to mind quickly. When someone sees something that investigative reporters should see, we want them to think of ProPublica.”.

    Up next for the team? Handing out coasters in sports bars to collect info on sports betting.
